transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-28
Time: 09:30 PT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Patel (Redwood AE), Marcus Lee (Redwood SE), Jamal Ortega (Redwood CSM); Dr. Emily Carter (CTO, Veridian), Rahul Singh (Cloud/Infra), Marta Ruiz (Head of Security), Leo Park (ML Lead)

Summary (auto):
Initial discovery for on-prem, air-gapped deployment of Redwood Private. Customer requirements: fully offline updates, strict data residency, HSM/KMS integration, SOC2/ISO constraints, limited rack-level GPUs (pref A100/H100), minimal external egress. Discussed offline update patterns, hardware mapping, fallback to Dedicated for non-sensitive workloads, and next steps to share playbook and worksheet.

Transcript:
[00:00] Sofia: hey everyone thanks for joining, this is sofia from redwood inference, i'm the AE on this account, i think we met briefly last week. how's everybody doing?
[00:08] Dr. Emily: good morning thanks, yes appreciate you fitting this in, we're trying to move quickly, lots of regulatory constraints so trying to walk through feasibility.
[00:14] Sofia: totally, we'll keep this focused. marcus is our solutions engineer, he'll do most of the technical deep dive. marcus do you want to intro?
[00:22] Marcus: hey all, marcus lee, redwood se. i'll try to map our architecture to your air-gapped reqs and talk about offline updates, kernel compatibility, and model variants.
[00:30] Rahul: quick context from our side - veridian has patient genomic datasets, everything must remain on-prem; no outbound network to the internet, period. We have a dedicated datacenter in boston, racks with 4x A100s in a couple of pods, and a smaller lab site with 1-2 H100s. We also have strict change control and monthly maintenance windows.
[00:55] Marcus: ok that helps. for air-gapped deployments we typically do a private control plane that can be run in your environment; you can opt for our turnkey bundle or we can hand over artifacts. updates are delivered as signed bundles that can be transported out-of-band - usb/external transfer or sequestered jump host.
[01:14] Marta: with respect to updates, we need to understand the signing/verification story, where keys live, and whether we can use our HSM for signing. we also have SSO/SAML for users and RBAC that needs to integrate with our LDAP.
[01:28] Marcus: yes, we support KMS integrations and can bring-your-own-key (BYOK) using an HSM. The offline update bundle is signed by redwood and can be re-signed by customer HSM during ingestion if you prefer. We maintain checksums and attestations.
[01:45] Leo: curious about model size and quantization. we currently run an internal LLM fine-tuned on our genomic nomenclature; do you recommend running float16 full models or quantized variants in air-gapped setups?
[01:58] Marcus: tradeoffs there - quantization (int8/4-bit) reduces memory and improves throughput, but there's a small risk to inference fidelity for genomic terms. we can ship quantized kernels and also provide a canary model to validate accuracy on your eval set.
[02:18] Dr. Emily: timeline wise, we want a POC by end of Q2, production by Q4. security sign-off is the gating item.
[02:25] Sofia: that seems doable, typical path is POC scoping then a pilot in one rack. we'll propose a hardware mapping and an eval plan.
[02:33] Rahul: one constraint - our network is using strict egress controls; nothing outbound except to a whitelisted patch server that is offline for most of the month. can redwood run entirely without control-plane egress?
[02:45] Marcus: yes, in private deployments we support fully isolated control plane. you can run with a local control plane that has no internet egress. the only thing to design is update delivery and telemetry - telemetry would be buffered and must be pulled only during maintenance windows if allowed.
[03:05] Marta: what about audit logs and traceability? we need immutable logs forwarded to our SIEM and retention for 7 years for certain workflows.
[03:14] Marcus: we can export audit logs to syslog or S3-compatible object stores inside your network. retention policies can be configured; for immutable logs we support write-once storage options via your object-store configuration.
[03:30] Rahul: hardware question - are there strict requirements for CPU/RAM per GPU? our racks are older, some nodes are NVL 3rd-gen, we're not sure about nvlink topologies.
[03:42] Marcus: typical recommended is x CPU per GPU for feeding tokens, but it depends on batch sizes and latency SLOs. For sequence lengths typical of your workloads, i'd start with A100 40GB equivalence and 96-256GB RAM per node. NVLink helps for multi-gpu KV cache, but with model sharding we can also support single-GPU per model serving if you avoid very large contexts.
[04:05] Leo: our models use long contexts (8k-32k), so KV cache will be large. how does redwood handle KV cache in on-prem with limited nvlink?
[04:14] Marcus: we have a couple strategies: local KV cache with periodic checkpointing, offloading to host memory, and cross-GPU sharding when nvlink is present. If nvlink isn't available, you'd see increased latency for cross-GPU attention; we can recommend quantized model variants and optimized kernel flags to mitigate.
[04:35] Dr. Emily: latency target for critical workflows is <200ms p95 for short queries, permissible up to 1s for longer genomics reads. is that realistic?
[04:45] Marcus: for short prompts with batching disabled and local models on A100/H100 that should be achievable. For long-context workloads you may see higher p95. we can benchmark during the POC with representative prompt sets.
[05:00] Sofia: from a product perspective we also provide routing policies - you could route sensitive patient requests to private on-prem and non-sensitive inference to our Dedicated hosted cluster to save cost. that's a common hybrid pattern.
[05:12] Rahul: that raises data flow questions - any data that touches Redwood hosted must be scrubbed, so we'd prefer that routing only happen if the dataset is non-pii.
[05:20] Sofia: understood. fine-grained routing by label is supported in the API or via your gateway.
[05:28] Marta: encryption at rest and in flight - do you require customer KMS? we prefer to manage keys in our HSM and never hand raw keys to vendors.
[05:36] Marcus: we support BYOK where keys stay in your HSM and redwood services run using wrapped keys. for air-gapped the control plane never sees unwrapped keys.
[05:45] Dr. Emily: compliance - do you have SOC 2 reports and ISO27k docs we can review?
[05:52] Jamal: yes we'll send SOC2 Type II and our security pack; for private deployments we provide additional documentation that maps to our product boundaries and what we recommend for your control plane.
[06:02] Rahul: can you talk through the offline update flow? how often are updates expected, and how do we validate them securely?
[06:10] Marcus: typical cadence is monthly security patches and model updates as needed. for air-gapped customers we produce signed bundles which you import. import happens in a staging environment, automated validation runs (checksums, signature verification, test inference runs against canary prompts), then promotion to prod during your maintenance window. If you want, we can also provide a physical media option.
[06:34] Marta: what differences are there between your private product and a 'bring-your-own' open runtime? i.e., if we run an open-source runtime ourselves, what's the additional value?
[06:43] Sofia: good question - Redwood Private includes the inference engine with performance optimizations, orchestration, automatic batching/caching, monitoring/trace hooks instrumented for model-level metrics, and the rollouts/rollback tools. the open runtimes miss the operational pieces: the rollout policies, model catalog, and the cost/perf tuning that our team supports.
[07:02] Leo: on the performance topic, do you recommend certain CUDA/cuDNN versions? we have some legacy firmware on the compute nodes.
[07:10] Marcus: we publish a compatibility matrix. recent H100/A100 kernels prefer CUDA 12.x and certain NCCL versions. for older nodes we can recommend CPU-optimized builds, but there are performance penalties. we'll include a compatibility spreadsheet in the worksheet.
[07:24] Dr. Emily: any constraints around offline telemetry? we want zero telemetry leaving the closed network by default.
[07:31] Marcus: default for air-gapped is no outbound telemetry. we can configure a pull model where logs are exported to a local S3 bucket and you decide when to share sanitized telemetry.
[07:41] Rahul: licensing and pricing - are there caps on request volume for private? how are upgrades handled?
[07:48] Sofia: private is licensed as an annual platform fee + per-node or per-GPU seat pricing. upgrades for new major features are delivered as opt-in bundles; security patches are included. for large model updates we can negotiate a transfer window and associated support.
[08:02] Marta: risk assessment - we need to know the blast radius if a model gets compromised or a key is leaked. how do you support key rotation and emergency revocation?
[08:11] Marcus: we support key rotation via HSM-based rewrapping and maintain revocation lists for bundles. emergency key revocation would require re-issuing signed bundles; we can support fast-path rotation during an incident.
[08:24] Leo: practical question - what does the POC look like? do you bring software and we run it, or do you come onsite to help run throughput tests?
[08:33] Sofia: we usually do remote-assisted POC for the first cut; for air-gapped customers we can send an SE onsite if needed for a week to help with network, storage, and tuning.
[08:42] Rahul: an onsite visit would help. also, for procurement we need an indemnity and data processing addendum to be in place.
[08:49] Jamal: we have standard enterprise contracts and an addendum for private deployments; we can start that process in parallel.
[08:55] Dr. Emily: how long to get initial deployment artifacts?
[08:58] Marcus: we can share the deployment playbook, the hardware worksheet, and the compatibility matrix within 48 business hours after the call.
[09:05] Sofia: great, i'll capture that as an action item.
[09:09] --[brief silence as notes are taken]--
[09:30] Marcus: diving a bit deeper on model lifecycle in air-gapped setups: we recommend separating control-plane metadata (models catalog/versions) from heavy binaries. binaries are delivered as signed OCI-style artifacts you pull into an internal registry. the metadata can be managed locally.
[09:50] Rahul: do you require container runtimes? we use a locked-down kubernetes distro with a readonly file system.
[09:57] Marcus: we support both OCI containers and bare-metal packages. for locked-down k8s we provide helm charts and also plain systemd units if containers are disallowed.
[10:07] Dr. Emily: for our ML team, we need to run custom builds of the model - can we bring our own model weights and run them on Redwood Private?
[10:15] Marcus: yes, BYO model weights is supported. we'll need to validate the model architecture for performance and provide guidance on kernel selection and quantization profiles.
[10:25] Leo: any gotchas with fine-tuned weights that reference external tokenizers or vocab assets?
[10:31] Marcus: you'd need to package all assets into the signed bundle. we have a bundling tool that picks up tokenizer artifacts and verifies checksums.
[10:39] Marta: security control question - can we enforce mandatory MFA for the console and audit who performed bundle imports?
[10:45] Marcus: yes, RBAC + SSO + MFA are supported; bundle import events are logged with user identity and can be forwarded to your SIEM.
[10:55] Rahul: network ports - what needs to be open between nodes? we need a one-pager for our firewall team.
[11:01] Marcus: i'll include a minimal ports diagram - typically intra-cluster gRPC and control-plane ports, plus optional metrics/ssh for debugging.
[11:09] Dr. Emily: curious about fallback - if a node fails, how graceful is degradation? we can't have long downtimes during clinical workflows.
[11:17] Marcus: Redwood runtime supports graceful degradation with model fallback policies; you can have a lower-cost quantized model act as a fallback, or route to a hot spare in another rack. we also support canary deploys and automatic rollback on error rates.
[11:33] Sofia: to recap the requirements we've heard so far: fully air-gapped control plane, BYOK/HSM integration, offline/signed bundle updates, immutable audit logs exportable to SIEM, monthly maintenance windows for upgrades, POC by end of Q2, hardware worksheet to map GPUs and nvlink, and decision on hybrid routing for non-PII workloads. is that accurate?
[11:55] Dr. Emily: yes that's correct.
[11:58] Rahul: add note about long-context workloads and KV cache sizing being critical.
[12:03] Sofia: noted. any red flags you see from our side, marcus?
[12:06] Marcus: main risk is older hardware topology lacking nvlink, which affects multi-gpu large-context performance. we can mitigate in software but need to set expectations.
[12:17] Leo: also want to stress accuracy regressions on quantized models for specialized genomic tokens - we'll need to validate on our eval set.
[12:25] Marcus: absolutely, we'll run a suite of evaluation prompts.
[12:29] Jamal: legal/procurement note - we'll share draft contract terms and DPA; we can align on the indemnity language.
[12:36] Dr. Emily: timeline for next meeting? we'd like a technical deep-dive with our infra team and security the week after next.
[12:42] Sofia: i'll propose times. marcus, can you lead the infra deep-dive?
[12:46] Marcus: yes happy to.
[12:48] --[pause]--
[30:00] [conversation continues - deeper technical Q&A and noise/interruptions occasionally]
[38:20] Rahul: one more thing on OS images - we prefer signed OS images. will redwood verify kernel modules?
[38:30] Marcus: we don't sign OS images but we support verifying runtime binaries and kernel modules included in the bundle. for strict environments you can do an additional layer of signing with your HSM.
[40:10] Marta: when we do onboarding, who has access to keys and secrets? how is least-privilege enforced?
[40:18] Marcus: least-privilege is enforced via RBAC, mTLS between services, and separation of roles in the control plane. keys are never stored unwrapped in the control plane for air-gapped installs.
[41:05] Sofia: final commercial note - typical entry point is a 3-month pilot with support hours and a defined scope of tests; after that, commit to private annual license if POC passes. are you comfortable with that path?
[41:20] Dr. Emily: yes that seems reasonable. we'll need an internal budget sign-off but pilot is the right next step.
[41:28] Leo: can you share target SLA numbers for private installs?
[41:33] Jamal: private SLAs vary by deployment - we'll propose an SLA for uptime and latency once we see the rack config. for pilots we usually promise response times and on-call support.
[41:45] Rahul: ok let's wrap up, please send the playbook and worksheet.
[41:50] Sofia: absolutely - summary & next steps to be emailed after the call. thanks everyone, and we'll follow up with proposed times for next week.
[41:58] Dr. Emily: thank you, appreciate it.
[42:02] Marta: thanks.
[42:05] [call ends]

Notes: transcript includes occasional minor transcription errors (e.g., 'KV cash' in older outputs) but core points captured.
